transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Yeah… I came in because I lost my temper on a board call. It was over a small question about the facility budget—nothing that should’ve set me off like that. I just snapped, and that’s not how I run my company, you know? I’ve spent years trying to keep a steady hand with people, even when the numbers get messy or someone’s asking the same question twice. I don’t treat people that way, or at least I don’t want to. So… that shook me enough to come here.
Have you been feeling more irritable or angry than usual, even outside of situations that might normally frustrate you?

Yeah… yes, I guess I have, or at least enough that it scared me. The board call is the thing that keeps playing back. It was such a small question about the facility budget, the kind of thing I’ve answered a hundred times, and I just… snapped.

And that’s not how I run my company. I’ve always tried to keep my voice level, even when people are circling the same issue. I mean, budgets are always like that—one number here, one repair there, someone wants to know why the roof costs what it costs—but I don’t usually take it out on people. This time I did. That’s what bothers me.
Have you noticed any other changes in your mood lately, like feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless exactly… but things feel kind of flat. Like, I’ll sit down with a chess problem—usually that steadies me, you know, makes my mind line up in neat little rows. Or I’ll look at my hiking notes, because I keep these notes from trails, mileage, weather, little things my wife says are too detailed… and lately it’s like I’m looking at someone else’s hobby.

Dinner with my wife too. Normally that’s the part of the day where I can put the company down for an hour, talk about normal things. But right now I know I should be enjoying it, and I just… can’t quite get there. It’s not that I don’t want to. It just doesn’t land the way it usually does.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, like chess problems or hiking?

Yeah… I have. Chess problems, my hiking notes, even dinner with my wife—those are usually the things that sort of bring me back to myself. I’ll sit there with a position on the board, and normally I’d get absorbed in it, but now it just feels… flat.

Same with the hiking notes. I used to care about every little detail—trail conditions, mileage, what the weather did—and now I look at it and it’s like paperwork. And dinner with my wife, I know I should be enjoying that time, but I just can’t seem to get there. It doesn’t feel the way it usually does.
Have you been feeling more tired or lacking energy lately, even when you haven’t been doing anything physically or mentally demanding?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I get tired, but who doesn’t at my age, right? Especially with the kind of days I have—although my wife says I blame everything on work, which… she may have a point.

But sitting still and suddenly feeling drained for no reason? I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed that in particular. My attention’s been on other things, honestly, so it’s hard to separate out what’s tired and what’s just… the day getting away from me.
Have you been having trouble sleeping lately—like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or waking up earlier than you intended?

I’m not sure I’ve really tracked it closely. Sleep is one of those things I tend to just… push through, I guess. My wife has always said I treat sleep like it’s optional, which probably isn’t fair, but when you’re running a company there’s always some email or some numbers you can look at one more time.

But lately? I don’t know. I can’t give you a clean answer like, “yes, I wake up at 3:00,” or anything like that. I haven’t noticed a specific pattern. Some nights are better than others, but I couldn’t say it’s been one particular kind of trouble.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently—like eating less than usual or losing weight without trying?

I haven’t really noticed anything definite there. My wife would probably know better than me—she’s the one who notices if I leave half a plate or if my belt’s sitting different, that kind of thing.

I mean, meals have been… a bit irregular, but they always are when work gets busy. I’ll forget lunch and then eat something stupid at four o’clock, or I’ll have coffee and call it breakfast, which I know isn’t exactly a health plan. But as far as losing weight without trying or suddenly not having an appetite, I can’t say I’ve seen that. Nothing that jumped out at me, anyway.
How long have you been feeling this way—this irritability, flatness, and loss of enjoyment—in total?

About six days, I think. Since the explosion and the fire during that walkthrough.

It’s funny—well, not funny—but I keep thinking about how that walkthrough was supposed to be routine. We’ve done a hundred of those, you know? You put on the vest, people nod, someone points at a gauge like everyone understands it… and then suddenly everything’s different.

So, yeah, if you’re asking how long I’ve been this way, I’d say it started then. Six days or so.
Can you tell me more about the explosion and fire during the walkthrough? How did that affect you?

It was… I mean, it was loud. That’s the first thing, I guess. We were near the loading area, and then there was the blast and the fire, and everything just went kind of chaotic.

I keep trying to get back to normal business—calls, spreadsheets, the usual headaches. Funny thing is, I’ve sat through worse quarterly reports than some disasters, you know, people acting like a two-percent miss is the end of the world. But now I’ll be in the middle of a call or looking at the numbers, and that blast and the fire just jump back into my head. Like a bad film I didn’t ask to see.

It doesn’t stay tidy, either. I’ll be trying to focus on margins or inventory, and suddenly I’m back there by the loading area for a second. Then I lose my place and have to pretend I was just checking something.
Have you been feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things that happened, like the explosion or anything else lately?

Guilty… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say that’s the word I’d use.

I mean, when something like that happens, everybody starts replaying things, don’t they? Who was standing where, who signed off on what, whether somebody should’ve pushed harder about some procedure. In business, you can spend six hours in a meeting arguing over whether a comma in a report changes responsibility—drives me crazy.

But blaming myself, like I caused it? No, I can’t really say that. I’m not sitting there thinking, “This was my fault.” It’s more just… noise in my head, going over pieces of it and not getting anywhere.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or on the contrary, feeling restless and unable to sit still, even when you’re not trying to be active?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that, exactly. I mean, I’m not pacing around the room like some cartoon executive waiting for a deal to close, and I don’t think I’m moving in slow motion either.

Although, you know, people always think executives are restless by nature—meetings, flights, someone handing you a folder before you’ve finished the last one. I’ve spent half my life being told to sit still in conference rooms while somebody explains a chart that could’ve been an email.

But for what you’re asking… no, I can’t really say I’ve noticed being slower or unable to sit still.
Have you lost interest or felt no pleasure in almost all activities, even those you used to enjoy?

Yeah… somewhat. I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped doing everything, exactly, but the things that usually sort of… settle me, they don’t seem to land right now.

Like I’ll sit down with a chess problem—used to clear my head, you know, just the board and the pieces, no committee arguing over the obvious—and now it’s just flat. Or my hiking notes, places I meant to go back to, little details about trails… normally I like that. Dinner with my wife, too. I know I should be enjoying it, and I want to, but I can’t quite get there. It’s like the feeling is behind glass or something.
Have you found that nothing gives you pleasure anymore, or that you’ve lost interest in almost everything, even things you used to care about?

Yeah, I mean… not nothing, exactly. That sounds a little too absolute. But the things that usually sort of steady me, they feel flat right now.

I’ll look at a chess problem, and normally I can get absorbed in it—like everything else gets quiet for a few minutes. Or I’ll go through my hiking notes, maps, little routes I wanted to try. Even dinner with my wife… I know I should be enjoying it, I want to enjoy it, but it’s like I can’t quite reach the feeling. Like it’s there behind glass.
Have you felt like nothing gives you pleasure anymore, or that you’ve lost interest in almost everything, even things you used to care about?

Yes… I think I have, though I keep wanting to qualify it because “nothing” sounds dramatic. It’s more like the usual things don’t reach me.

A chess problem, for instance—that used to calm me down. You’d think a board with sixty-four squares wouldn’t do much, but there’s something orderly about it, unlike half the meetings I’ve sat through where everyone talks and nobody moves a piece. And my hiking notes, the routes and little plans I used to like going over… they just sit there now.

Even dinner with my wife, which I know should feel good, feels kind of flat. I can tell myself I should enjoy it, but I can’t quite get there. Like the pleasure is nearby, but behind glass.
Would you say that you’ve completely lost pleasure in the things you used to enjoy, or do some of them still bring you at least a little enjoyment, even if it’s less than before?

Not completely, no… I don’t think I’d say it’s gone altogether. It’s more that the things that usually settle me just feel sort of flat right now.

Like I’ll sit with a chess problem, and normally there’s a little satisfaction in seeing the pattern—like when a plan finally works in a boardroom, except quieter and with fewer people pretending they invented it. But lately it doesn’t really land. Same with my hiking notes, those little trail details I used to enjoy fussing over.

And dinner with my wife… I know that should feel good. I want it to. But I can’t quite get there. It’s like the enjoyment is still somewhere nearby, but I’m not reaching it.
Would you say that you’ve completely lost pleasure in the things you used to enjoy, or do some of them still bring you at least a little enjoyment, even if it’s less than before?

Not completely gone, no. I mean, I can still recognize that something ought to be enjoyable, if that makes sense.

Like with a chess problem—I’ll sit there and look at it, and normally that sort of thing settles me. Same with my hiking notes, the routes and little details. I used to get a quiet kind of pleasure out of that. And dinner with my wife, too. It isn’t that I don’t care about those things.

It’s just… they feel flat right now. Like I know I should enjoy them, but I can’t quite get there.
Would you say that you’re experiencing no pleasure at all in the things you used to enjoy, or is there still some pleasure, even if it’s less than before?

There’s still some, I suppose, but it’s faint. Not no pleasure at all. More like… the volume is turned down.

The things that usually settle me—chess problems, my hiking notes, even just dinner with my wife—they’re still there, and I know they should feel good. I can look at the chessboard and think, well, this used to quiet my head. I remember once spending half a Sunday on one position, which my wife thought was ridiculous, but I liked the order of it.

Now it just feels flat. Like I’m trying to get to the feeling and I can’t quite reach it.
Would you say that you’re experiencing no pleasure at all in the things you used to enjoy, or is there still some pleasure, even if it’s less than before?

No, not no pleasure at all… I wouldn’t put it that strongly. It’s more that the things that usually help me feel like myself just don’t quite connect right now.

Like a chess problem—I can still sit there and know, intellectually, that I used to enjoy figuring it out. Or my hiking notes, the little route details and the mileage and all that. I used to get a sort of calm from that, which sounds dull when I say it out loud, but it mattered. And dinner with my wife… that should feel good.

It just feels flat. Like I know the enjoyment is supposed to be there, but I can’t quite get to it.

inference_history.note: The patient's report of feeling flat, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities (e.g., chess, hiking notes), and reduced enjoyment in social interactions (e.g., dinner with wife) suggests depressive symptoms. This shifts focus toward affective disorders, particularly depressive episodes and recurrent depressive disorder. It rules out some personality disorders from the previous list (e.g., F60.0-F60.9) as the primary concern, given the mood-congruent presentation.

The patient's symptoms continue to point toward a depressive disorder. The persistent anhedonia, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, and emotional flattening support the inclusion of depressive disorders, including both major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.20) is ruled out due to the duration and pervasiveness of symptoms beyond a typical adjustment reaction.

The patient's symptoms have persisted for approximately six days, following a traumatic event (the explosion and fire). While the duration is still relatively short, the severity of the depressive symptoms (loss of pleasure in almost all activities, emotional flatness, irritability) and their persistence point toward a moderate to severe major depressive episode (F32.2–F32.3). Recurrent depressive disorder (F33.2–F33.3) remains a possibility if this evolves into a pattern of repeated episodes. The lack of clear psychomotor changes, significant sleep disturbance, or weight/appetite changes prevents full specification of severity in some categories, but current presentation most closely aligns with the remaining candidates.

Recurrent depressive disorder (F33.2–F33.3) remains a possibility if this evolves into a pattern of repeated episodes. The lack of clear psychomotor changes, significant sleep disturbance, or weight/appetite changes prevents full specification of severity in some categories, but current presentation most closely aligns with the remaining candidates.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of pleasure in all or almost all activities, indicating anhedonia.
doctor.question: Would you say that you’ve completely lost pleasure in the things you used to enjoy, or do some of them still bring you at least a little enjoyment, even if it’s less than before?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: Things that usually settle me, like a chess problem, my hiking notes, or dinner with my wife, just feel flat right now, like I know I should enjoy them but I can't get there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether previously enjoyable activities still bring pleasure or whether pleasure is completely lost, which directly matches inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Not completely, no… I don’t think I’d say it’s gone altogether. It’s more that the things that usually settle me just feel sort of flat right now.

Like I’ll sit with a chess problem, and normally there’s a little satisfaction in seeing the pattern—like when a plan finally works in a boardroom, except quieter and with fewer people pretending they invented it. But lately it doesn’t really land. Same with my hiking notes, those little trail details I used to enjoy fussing over.

And dinner with my wife… I know that should feel good. I want it to. But I can’t quite get there. It’s like the enjoyment is still somewhere nearby, but I’m not reaching it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a complete loss of pleasure in previously enjoyable activities, which would help differentiate between major depressive episodes and a normal stress response.
doctor.question: Would you say that you’ve completely lost pleasure in the things you used to enjoy, or do some of them still bring you at least a little enjoyment, even if it’s less than before?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: Things that usually settle me, like a chess problem, my hiking notes, or dinner with my wife, just feel flat right now, like I know I should enjoy them but I can't get there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether pleasure and enjoyment in previously enjoyable activities are completely absent or only reduced, which directly matches difficulty experiencing positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Not completely gone, no. I mean, I can still recognize that something ought to be enjoyable, if that makes sense.

Like with a chess problem—I’ll sit there and look at it, and normally that sort of thing settles me. Same with my hiking notes, the routes and little details. I used to get a quiet kind of pleasure out of that. And dinner with my wife, too. It isn’t that I don’t care about those things.

It’s just… they feel flat right now. Like I know I should enjoy them, but I can’t quite get there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of pleasure in almost all activities, a key symptom for major depressive disorder severity.
doctor.question: Would you say that you’re experiencing no pleasure at all in the things you used to enjoy, or is there still some pleasure, even if it’s less than before?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: Things that usually settle me, like a chess problem, my hiking notes, or dinner with my wife, just feel flat right now, like I know I should enjoy them but I can't get there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether previously enjoyable activities now bring no pleasure or reduced pleasure, which matches inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
There’s still some, I suppose, but it’s faint. Not no pleasure at all. More like… the volume is turned down.

The things that usually settle me—chess problems, my hiking notes, even just dinner with my wife—they’re still there, and I know they should feel good. I can look at the chessboard and think, well, this used to quiet my head. I remember once spending half a Sunday on one position, which my wife thought was ridiculous, but I liked the order of it.

Now it just feels flat. Like I’m trying to get to the feeling and I can’t quite reach it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of pleasure in most activities, a key symptom of major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Would you say that you’re experiencing no pleasure at all in the things you used to enjoy, or is there still some pleasure, even if it’s less than before?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions

patient.answer:
No, not no pleasure at all… I wouldn’t put it that strongly. It’s more that the things that usually help me feel like myself just don’t quite connect right now.

Like a chess problem—I can still sit there and know, intellectually, that I used to enjoy figuring it out. Or my hiking notes, the little route details and the mileage and all that. I used to get a sort of calm from that, which sounds dull when I say it out loud, but it mattered. And dinner with my wife… that should feel good.

It just feels flat. Like I know the enjoyment is supposed to be there, but I can’t quite get to it.

While there are features of anhedonia and irritability, the short duration and clear temporal relationship to a psychosocial stressor make a diagnosis of major depressive disorder unlikely.
